questions.sec: Portal hypertension: clinical significance and pathogenesis · p1001
questions.q: ‘Portal hypertension occurs only in the presence of cirrhosis.’
opts: False — it occurs exclusively without cirrhosis
True, but only in post-hepatic forms
False — it can manifest with or without cirrhosis
True — cirrhosis is a mandatory prerequisite
questions.exp: Opening line of the chapter: portal hypertension can manifest with or without cirrhosis. (Book p1001)

questions.sec: Portal hypertension: clinical significance and pathogenesis · p1001
questions.q: Match the p1001 outcome chains — 1) Portal hypertension  2) Ascites  3) Jaundice + liver failure  4) Raised splenic pressure … A) Average survival without transplant printed as ‘a years’  B) Leads to hepatorenal syndrome  C) Hepatic encephalopathy and variceal bleeding  D) Splenomegaly and thrombocytopenia
questions.exp: Portal hypertension leads to hepatic encephalopathy, variceal bleeding and ascites; ascites (1st sign of decompensation) leads to hepatorenal syndrome; jaundice + liver failure = decompensation with average survival ‘a years’ without transplant as printed; raised splenic pressure gives splenomegaly and thrombocytopenia. (Book p1001)

questions.sec: Portal hypertension: clinical significance and pathogenesis · p1001
questions.q: The 1st sign of decompensation in portal hypertension is:
questions.exp: Under the bullet ‘ascites’ the page states ‘1st sign of decompensation’. (Book p1001)

questions.sec: Portal hypertension: clinical significance and pathogenesis · p1001
questions.q: Portal hypertension is defined by a portal venous pressure of:
questions.exp: Pathogenesis line: portal venous pressure ≥ 12 mm Hg. (Book p1001)

questions.sec: Portal hypertension: clinical significance and pathogenesis · p1001
questions.q: Sinusoidal pressure is defined as ≥ 6 mm Hg; it becomes clinically significant at:
questions.exp: ‘Sinusoidal pressure ≥ 6 mm Hg (clinically significant if ≥ 10 mm Hg)’. (Book p1001)

questions.sec: Portal hypertension: clinical significance and pathogenesis · p1001
questions.q: A 48-year-old with biopsy-proven cirrhosis has a spleen 4 cm below the costal margin and a platelet count of 90,000/µL. Which pair gives the earliest clinical and earliest biochemical manifestations of portal hypertension?
questions.exp: Raised splenic pressure → splenomegaly (earliest clinical) and thrombocytopenia (earliest biochemical). (Book p1001)

questions.sec: Portal hypertension: clinical significance and pathogenesis · p1001
questions.q: The mean survival without decompensation or transplant in portal hypertension is:
questions.exp: ‘Mean survival without decompensation / transplant : 12 years’. (Book p1001)

questions.sec: Portal hypertension: clinical significance and pathogenesis · p1001
questions.q: After decompensation (jaundice + liver failure), average survival without transplant is about:
questions.exp: The page prints ‘Decompensation : Average survival a years without transplant’ — the ‘a’ is a typographical slip for 1, i.e. about 1 year, in contrast to the 12 years without decompensation. (Book p1001)

questions.sec: Portal hypertension: clinical significance and pathogenesis · p1001
questions.q: All but one of the following are listed under ‘Portal hypertension leads to’. The odd one out is:
questions.exp: The three listed consequences are hepatic encephalopathy, variceal bleeding and ascites; hepatomegaly is not listed. (Book p1001)

questions.sec: Portal hypertension: clinical significance and pathogenesis · p1001
questions.q: ‘Thrombocytopenia is the earliest clinical manifestation of portal hypertension.’
opts: True — thrombocytopenia is the earliest clinical manifestation of portal hypertension
False — both findings are biochemical rather than clinical manifestations
True — but only when splenic vein thrombosis is present alongside cirrhosis
False — splenomegaly is the earliest clinical, thrombocytopenia the earliest biochemical
questions.exp: Raised splenic pressure → splenomegaly (earliest clinical) and thrombocytopenia (earliest biochemical). (Book p1001)

questions.sec: The cirrhotic sinusoid: diagram labels · p1001
questions.q: Match the cirrhotic-sinusoid diagram events of p1001 to the structures — 1) Deposition of collagen  2) Activation  3) Constriction  4) Defenestration … A) Sinusoids  B) Hepatic stellate cells  C) Space of Disse  D) Sinusoidal lumen/fenestrae
questions.exp: Diagram labels: deposition of collagen in space of Disse; activation of hepatic stellate cells; constriction of sinusoids; defenestration of sinusoids. (Book p1001)

questions.sec: The cirrhotic sinusoid: diagram labels · p1001
questions.q: In cirrhosis, collagen deposition in the hepatic sinusoid occurs in the:
questions.exp: The diagram labels ‘Deposition of collagen in space of Disse’. (Book p1001)

questions.sec: The cirrhotic sinusoid: diagram labels · p1001
questions.q: Which cell is labelled as activated in the cirrhotic sinusoid of p1001?
questions.exp: ‘Activation of hepatic stellate cells’ is labelled in the cirrhotic panel. (Book p1001)

questions.sec: The cirrhotic sinusoid: diagram labels · p1001
questions.q: ‘Fenestrae of the sinusoidal endothelium are preserved in cirrhosis.’
opts: False — fenestrae are lost only in Budd–Chiari
True, but only in the pericentral zone
questions.exp: The cirrhotic panel labels ‘Defenestration of sinusoids’ and the summary line reads ‘Disappearance of fenestration in cirrhosis’. (Book p1001)

questions.sec: The cirrhotic sinusoid: diagram labels · p1001
questions.q: In a cirrhotic liver, the direct mechanical mechanism by which regenerating nodules raise portal pressure, as drawn on p1001, is:
opts: Compression of sinusoids by nodules and fibrous septae
Stenosis of hepatic veins by nodules
questions.exp: ‘Nodule and fibrous septation compress sinusoids → leads to ↑ portal pressure → ↑ splenic vein pressure’. (Book p1001)

questions.sec: Hepatic vasculature: the portal vein · p1001
questions.q: The portal vein is formed behind the neck of the pancreas by the junction of the splenic vein and the:
questions.exp: Formation: splenic vein and superior mesenteric veins join behind the neck of pancreas. (Book p1001)

questions.sec: Hepatic vasculature: the portal vein · p1001
questions.q: The portal vein develops from the:
opts: Inferior segment of the left and right vitelline veins
Superior segment of the left and right vitelline veins
questions.exp: Development: ‘Inferior segment of left and right vitelline veins joins to form portal vein’. (Book p1001)

questions.sec: Hepatic vasculature: the portal vein · p1001
questions.q: The length of the portal vein given on p1001 is:
questions.exp: Under formation: ‘7.5 cm long’. (Book p1001)

questions.sec: Hepatic vasculature: the portal vein · p1001
questions.q: The haemodynamic character of the portal vein stated on p1001 is:
questions.exp: ‘Portal vein has high compliance low resistance’. (Book p1001)

questions.sec: Hepatic vasculature: the portal vein · p1001
questions.q: Match the portal-branching diagram labels of p1001 — 1) Umbilical vein  2) Cystic vein  3) 1st order portal vein  4) 3rd order portal vein (Bifurcation) … A) Bifurcates in the lobe  B) Main trunk  C) Drains into the right portal vein  D) Drains into the left portal vein
questions.exp: ‘Umbilical vein drains into left portal vein’, ‘Cystic vein drains into right portal vein’, 1st order portal vein is the main trunk, and the 3rd order portal vein carries the (Bifurcation) label. (Book p1001)

questions.sec: Hepatic vasculature: the portal vein · p1001
questions.q: Hepatic ischaemia remains rare in portal hypertension because of the hepatic buffer response — its basis on p1001 is:
opts: Arterialisation of portal inflow at the sinusoidal level
Dual blood supply of the liver (portal vein + hepatic artery)
Dilatation of the vasa recta around the central vein
Collateral flow through the paraumbilical veins
questions.exp: Note: hepatic buffer response — hepatic ischaemia is rare d/t dual blood supply, portal vein / hepatic artery. (Book p1001)

questions.sec: Hepatic vasculature: the portal vein · p1001
questions.q: At the hilum, the portal vein lies with respect to the hepatic artery and bile duct — the relation stated on p1001 is:
opts: Anterior to the hepatic artery and bile duct
Medial to the bile duct and anterior to the hepatic artery
Lateral to both the hepatic artery and bile duct
Posterior to the hepatic artery and bile duct
questions.exp: Under formation: ‘Hilum posterior to hepatic and bile duct’ — the portal vein lies posterior to the hepatic artery and bile duct. (Book p1001)

questions.sec: Sinusoidal vasoconstriction and the HVPG ladder · p1002
questions.q: In the equation P = F × R used on p1002 for portal HTN, a rise in sinusoidal resistance leads to:
opts: Rise in flow for fixed resistance
Fall in flow at fixed pressure
questions.exp: Resistance due to: (P = F × R; R↑ = P↑). (Book p1002)

questions.sec: Sinusoidal vasoconstriction and the HVPG ladder · p1002
questions.q: Match the HVPG (hepatic venous pressure gradient) ladder of p1002 — 1) 1–5 mm Hg  2) ≥ 10 mm Hg  3) ≥ 12 mm Hg  4) ≥ 20 mm Hg … A) Threshold pressure for variceal rupture  B) Normal value  C) ↑ Risk of death  D) Clinically significant portal hypertension
questions.exp: HVPG table: 1–5 mm Hg = normal value; ≥ 10 mm Hg = clinically significant portal hypertension; ≥ 12 mm Hg = threshold pressure for variceal rupture; ≥ 20 mm Hg = ↑ risk of death. (Book p1002)

questions.sec: Sinusoidal vasoconstriction and the HVPG ladder · p1002
questions.q: The HVPG that marks the threshold pressure for variceal rupture is:
questions.exp: ≥ 12 mm Hg is labelled the threshold pressure for variceal rupture. (Book p1002)

questions.sec: Sinusoidal vasoconstriction and the HVPG ladder · p1002
questions.q: A cirrhotic patient's HVPG is measured at 11 mm Hg. According to the p1002 ladder, the best interpretation is:
opts: Normal — HVPG must reach 12 mm Hg before portal hypertension is significant
Already within the ≥ 20 mm Hg band that marks an increased risk of death
Indeterminate — the 10–12 mm Hg gap on the ladder carries no printed label
Clinically significant portal hypertension, but below the printed variceal-rupture threshold
questions.exp: ≥ 10 mm Hg = clinically significant portal hypertension; ≥ 12 mm Hg = threshold for variceal rupture; so 11 sits between the two printed marks. (Book p1002)

questions.sec: Sinusoidal vasoconstriction and the HVPG ladder · p1002
questions.q: The functional (non-mechanical) cause of sinusoidal vasoconstriction in portal HTN is a fall in:
questions.exp: Functional cause: ↓ intrasinusoidal NO → contraction of sinusoid → defenestration. (Book p1002)

questions.sec: Sinusoidal vasoconstriction and the HVPG ladder · p1002
questions.q: ‘In sinusoidal vasoconstriction, the NO pathway causes the sinusoid to relax.’
opts: False — the cause is a rise, not a fall, in NO
True, but only in the presinusoidal segment
False — ↓ intrasinusoidal NO causes contraction of the sinusoid
True — NO mediates sinusoidal relaxation here
questions.exp: Functional cause: ↓ intrasinusoidal NO → contraction of sinusoid → defenestration. (Book p1002)

questions.sec: Sinusoidal vasoconstriction and the HVPG ladder · p1002
questions.q: The mechanical cause of sinusoidal resistance in portal HTN, as drawn on p1002, is:
opts: Spasm of the portal vein wall
questions.exp: Mechanical cause: nodule compressing sinusoid (functional arm is the ↓ NO pathway). (Book p1002)

questions.sec: Sinusoidal vasoconstriction and the HVPG ladder · p1002
questions.q: All but one of the following appear in the p1002 functional-cause chain (↓ intrasinusoidal NO → …). The odd one out is:
questions.exp: The chain is ↓ intrasinusoidal NO → contraction of sinusoid → defenestration; portal vein thrombosis is not part of it. (Book p1002)

questions.sec: Causes of portal HTN: pre-hepatic and post-hepatic · p1002
questions.q: Pre-hepatic portal hypertension corresponds to occlusion of the:
opts: The sinusoids themselves, as in the cirrhotic pattern
1st order portal vein (AKA extrahepatic portal venous obstruction, EHPVO)
3rd order portal vein, the intrahepatic branching point
Hepatic vein outflow (the Budd–Chiari, post-hepatic territory)
questions.exp: Pre-hepatic: first order portal vein occlusion AKA extrahepaticportal venous obstruction (EHPVO). (Book p1002)

questions.sec: Causes of portal HTN: pre-hepatic and post-hepatic · p1002
questions.q: EHPVO is characteristically seen in:
questions.exp: Pre-hepatic (EHPVO) — ‘seen in 3-8 yr olds’. (Book p1002)

questions.sec: Causes of portal HTN: pre-hepatic and post-hepatic · p1002
questions.q: Match the printed features of EHPVO — 1) Bleed  2) Spleen  3) Liver  4) Prognosis … A) No cirrhosis  B) Massive splenomegaly  C) Severe upper gastrointestinal  D) Good
questions.exp: Characteristic features: severe upper gastrointestinal bleed, massive splenomegaly; no cirrhosis (good prognosis). (Book p1002)

questions.sec: Causes of portal HTN: pre-hepatic and post-hepatic · p1002
questions.q: Post-hepatic portal hypertension, cause ‘a’, is hepatic vein obstruction, also known as:
questions.exp: Post-hepatic a. cause: hepatic vein obstruction AKA Budd Chiari syndrome. (Book p1002)

questions.sec: Causes of portal HTN: pre-hepatic and post-hepatic · p1002
questions.q: The classical findings of Budd–Chiari syndrome printed on p1002 are ascites and:
questions.exp: Classical findings: ascites, hepatomegaly (note: hepatomegaly, not splenomegaly). (Book p1002)

questions.sec: Causes of portal HTN: pre-hepatic and post-hepatic · p1002
questions.q: Match the post-hepatic ‘other causes’ (right heart failure) of p1002 — 1) Valvular  2) Myocardial  3) Pericardial … A) Constrictive pericarditis (↑ JVP)  B) Restrictive cardiomyopathy  C) Tricuspid regurgitation
questions.exp: Right heart failure: tricuspid regurgitation, restrictive cardiomyopathy, constrictive pericarditis (↑ JVP). (Book p1002)

questions.sec: Causes of portal HTN: pre-hepatic and post-hepatic · p1002
questions.q: A patient with constrictive pericarditis and a raised JVP develops ascites and portal pressure elevation. In the p1002 classification this falls under:
questions.exp: Constrictive pericarditis (↑ JVP) is listed under post-hepatic → b. other causes → right heart failure. (Book p1002)

questions.sec: Causes of portal HTN: pre-hepatic and post-hepatic · p1002
questions.q: Which of the following is the RARE cause of EHPVO listed on p1002?
questions.exp: Causes: umbilical sepsis (listed without qualifier) and splenic vein thrombosis (rare). (Book p1002)

questions.sec: Intrahepatic causes: pre-sinusoidal, post-sinusoidal, sinusoidal · p1002
questions.q: In the p1002 diagram, the intrahepatic branch of portal HTN is drawn at the level of the:
questions.exp: The arrow from ‘Intrahepatic’ is labelled (3rd order portal vein) and then splits into pre-sinusoidal, post-sinusoidal and sinusoidal. (Book p1002)

questions.sec: Intrahepatic causes: pre-sinusoidal, post-sinusoidal, sinusoidal · p1002
questions.q: Intrahepatic pre-sinusoidal cause ‘a’ is NCPF, which stands for:
opts: Non coagulative portal fibrosis of the portal tracts
Nodular confluent portal fibrosis with sinusoidal obliteration
Normocellular portal fibrosis of unknown aetiology
Non cirrhotic portal fibrosis (also idiopathic portal hypertension)
questions.exp: Pre-sinusoidal a. NCPF (Non cirrhotic portal fibrosis) / Idiopathic portal hypertension. (Book p1002)

questions.sec: Intrahepatic causes: pre-sinusoidal, post-sinusoidal, sinusoidal · p1002
questions.q: NCPF / idiopathic portal hypertension typically presents as a young adult with upper GI bleed and splenomegaly, and cirrhosis is:
questions.exp: Presentation: young adult with upper GI bleed, splenomegaly, cirrhosis (rare). (Book p1002)

questions.sec: Intrahepatic causes: pre-sinusoidal, post-sinusoidal, sinusoidal · p1002
questions.q: A day 20 post-allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant patient on a myeloablative alkylator-based regimen develops tender hepatomegaly and weight gain. The p1002 entity to suspect is:
opts: Budd–Chiari syndrome with hepatic vein thrombosis
questions.exp: Post-sinusoidal cause: sinusoidal obstruction syndrome / veno-occlusive disease a/w post hematopoietic stem cell transplant following myeloablative therapy with alkylating agents. (Book p1002)

questions.sec: Intrahepatic causes: pre-sinusoidal, post-sinusoidal, sinusoidal · p1002
questions.q: After myeloablative therapy with alkylating agents, symptoms of veno-occlusive disease appear:
questions.exp: The diagram shows the arrow labelled (10 – 30 days after) leading to symptoms. (Book p1002)

questions.sec: Intrahepatic causes: pre-sinusoidal, post-sinusoidal, sinusoidal · p1002
questions.q: All but one of the following are listed as intrahepatic pre-sinusoidal causes on p1002. The odd one out is:
questions.exp: Pre-sinusoidal: NCPF/idiopathic portal hypertension, schistosomiasis, sarcoidosis. Budd–Chiari is post-hepatic, not intrahepatic pre-sinusoidal. (Book p1002)

questions.sec: Intrahepatic causes: pre-sinusoidal, post-sinusoidal, sinusoidal · p1002
questions.q: The intrahepatic sinusoidal cause of portal hypertension on p1002 is:
questions.exp: Sinusoidal: cause — cirrhosis (post-sinusoidal is SOS/VOD; pre-sinusoidal is NCPF etc.). (Book p1002)

questions.sec: Intrahepatic causes: pre-sinusoidal, post-sinusoidal, sinusoidal · p1002
questions.q: The granulomatous ‘other cause’ of intrahepatic pre-sinusoidal portal HTN on p1002 is:
questions.exp: b. Other causes: schistosomiasis (parasitic) and sarcoidosis (granulomatous). (Book p1002)

questions.sec: Work-up flow of portal HTN and the HVPG measurement · p1003
questions.q: In the p1003 work-up flow, the step ‘Deranged LFT + USG : fatty liver + negative serology’ is qualified by:
questions.exp: Flow: deranged LFT + USG : fatty liver + negative serology (AST / ALT < 150) → confirms chronic hepatitis (NASH). (Book p1003)

questions.sec: Work-up flow of portal HTN and the HVPG measurement · p1003
questions.q: The Fibroscan value in the p1003 flow that leads to the diagnosis of cirrhosis is:
questions.exp: Flow: confirms chronic hepatitis (NASH) → Fibroscan : 13.5 kPa → cirrhosis. (Book p1003)

questions.sec: Work-up flow of portal HTN and the HVPG measurement · p1003
questions.q: After cirrhosis is established in the flow, the pair of findings that establishes portal hypertension (+) is:
questions.exp: Flow: cirrhosis → splenomegaly (+), ↓ platelet → portal hypertension (+). (Book p1003)

questions.sec: Work-up flow of portal HTN and the HVPG measurement · p1003
questions.q: Portal HTN is quantified with HVPG, where:
questions.exp: Quantity with HVPG: HVPG = WHVP − FHVP. (Book p1003)

questions.sec: Work-up flow of portal HTN and the HVPG measurement · p1003
questions.q: Match the p1003 abbreviations — 1) HVPG  2) WHVP  3) FHVP … A) Wedged hepatic venous pressure  B) Free hepatic venous pressure  C) Hepatic venous pressure gradient
questions.exp: HVPG : hepatic venous pressure gradient; WHVP : wedged hepatic venous pressure; FHVP : free hepatic venous pressure. (Book p1003)

questions.sec: Work-up flow of portal HTN and the HVPG measurement · p1003
questions.q: ‘On p1003 the expansion line prints the free pressure as “FWVP : Free hepatic venous pressure”, while the formula line prints HVPG = WHVP − FHVP.’
opts: False — the formula line prints FWVP
True, but the values are different concepts
True — the two printings differ (FWVP vs FHVP)
questions.exp: The expansion line is printed ‘FWVP : Free hepatic venous pressure’ whereas the formula is ‘HVPG = WHVP − FHVP’; both denote the free hepatic venous pressure. (Book p1003)

questions.sec: Work-up flow of portal HTN and the HVPG measurement · p1003
questions.q: A child with EHPVO has large oesophageal varices but a normal HVPG. Which row of the p1003 table explains why HVPG fails here?
opts: Prehepatic row — WHVP, FHVP and HVPG all normal
Postsinusoidal row — WHVP increased, FHVP normal
questions.exp: Prehepatic: normal / normal / normal — the gradient across the liver is normal because the obstruction is before the liver. (Book p1003)

questions.sec: Work-up flow of portal HTN and the HVPG measurement · p1003
questions.q: ‘In the p1003 flow, portal hypertension (+) is established only by endoscopy.’
opts: False — Fibroscan 13.5 kPa alone establishes the diagnosis of portal hypertension
True, but only when the HVPG arm is not performed in the same session
False — it follows cirrhosis with splenomegaly (+) and ↓ platelet; endoscopy is one of two follow-up arms
True — endoscopy is the sole step that establishes portal hypertension (+)
questions.exp: Flow: cirrhosis → splenomegaly (+), ↓ platelet → portal hypertension (+), which then branches to quantity with HVPG and endoscopy. (Book p1003)

questions.sec: The WHVP / FHVP / HVPG table read row by row · p1003
questions.q: Match the p1003 table locations with their pressure patterns — 1) Presinusoidal  2) Sinusoidal  3) The row where the hepatic vein cannot be cannulated … A) WHVP increased, FHVP increased, HVPG normal  B) WHVP, FHVP and HVPG all normal  C) WHVP increased, FHVP normal, HVPG increased
questions.exp: Presinusoidal: normal/normal/normal; sinusoidal: increased/normal/increased; the unlabeled row: increased / increased (hepatic vein cannot be cannulated) / normal. (Book p1003)

questions.sec: The WHVP / FHVP / HVPG table read row by row · p1003
questions.q: The prehepatic and presinusoidal rows of the p1003 table are identical: WHVP, FHVP and HVPG are all:
questions.exp: Both the prehepatic and presinusoidal rows print Normal in all three columns. (Book p1003)

questions.sec: The WHVP / FHVP / HVPG table read row by row · p1003
questions.q: In the sinusoidal (cirrhotic) row of the table, WHVP is increased while FHVP remains:
questions.exp: Sinusoidal: WHVP increased, FHVP normal, HVPG increased. (Book p1003)

questions.sec: The WHVP / FHVP / HVPG table read row by row · p1003
questions.q: In a patient with Budd–Chiari syndrome the hepatic vein cannot be cannulated. Which p1003 table row fits this situation, and what does it predict for HVPG?
opts: The unlabeled row — WHVP and FHVP increased, HVPG normal
The presinusoidal row — HVPG normal with all pressures normal
questions.exp: The unlabeled row: WHVP increased, FHVP increased (hepatic vein cannot be cannulated), HVPG normal — the pattern of post-hepatic obstruction. (Book p1003)

questions.sec: The WHVP / FHVP / HVPG table read row by row · p1003
questions.q: ‘In presinusoidal portal hypertension the HVPG is increased according to the p1003 table.’
opts: False — the WHVP is increased instead
False — presinusoidal: WHVP, FHVP and HVPG are all normal
questions.exp: Presinusoidal row: normal / normal / normal. (Book p1003)

questions.sec: The WHVP / FHVP / HVPG table read row by row · p1003
questions.q: In the p1003 flow, an HVPG > 10 mm Hg prompts Rx with the non-selective β-blocker labelled (best):
questions.exp: Bracket on the table: > 10 mm Hg → Rx non-selective β-blocker : carvedilol (best). (Book p1003)

questions.sec: Endoscopy, variceal ligation indications and modified Child–Pugh · p1003
questions.q: Endoscopy showing large varices → p1003 Rx of choice is the non-selective β-blocker:
questions.exp: Large varices → Rx non-selective β-blocker : carvedilol (best). (Book p1003)

questions.sec: Endoscopy, variceal ligation indications and modified Child–Pugh · p1003
questions.q: Endoscopy showing mild/moderate varices is handled by:
questions.exp: Endoscopy arms: large varices → non-selective β-blocker; mild/moderate varices → conservative management. (Book p1003)

questions.sec: Endoscopy, variceal ligation indications and modified Child–Pugh · p1003
questions.q: Match the p1003 indications for endoscopic variceal ligation — 1) Intolerant to β-blocker therapy  2) β-blockers contraindicated  3) Target HVPG not achieved … A) With β-blocker  B) Severe bradycardia  C) Asthma, COPD
questions.exp: Intolerant to β-blocker therapy: asthma, COPD; β-blockers contraindicated: severe bradycardia; target HVPG not achieved with β-blocker. (Book p1003)

questions.sec: Endoscopy, variceal ligation indications and modified Child–Pugh · p1003
questions.q: A cirrhotic with large varices develops a resting heart rate of 42 bpm after starting a β-blocker. According to p1003, endoscopic variceal ligation is indicated here under which heading?
questions.exp: Severe bradycardia is the printed example under ‘β-blockers contraindicated’; intolerance refers to asthma/COPD. (Book p1003)

questions.sec: Endoscopy, variceal ligation indications and modified Child–Pugh · p1003
questions.q: Match the modified Child–Pugh parameters of p1003 — 1) Ascites  2) Encephalopathy  3) Albumin  4) Prothrombin time … A) Seconds increased  B) Hepatic synthetic protein  C) Fluid in the peritoneal cavity  D) Altered sensorium
questions.exp: Parameters assessed: ascites, encephalopathy, bilirubin, albumin, prothrombin time (seconds increased). (Book p1003)

questions.sec: Endoscopy, variceal ligation indications and modified Child–Pugh · p1003
questions.q: In the modified Child–Pugh classes A, B, C of p1003, the bracketed classes that require transplant are:
opts: All three classes (A, B and C)
questions.exp: Classes: A, B, C — the bracket over B and C is annotated ‘Requires transplant’. (Book p1003)

questions.sec: Endoscopy, variceal ligation indications and modified Child–Pugh · p1003
questions.q: All but one of the following are parameters of the modified Child–Pugh system on p1003. The odd one out is:
questions.exp: Parameters: ascites, encephalopathy, bilirubin, albumin, prothrombin time (seconds increased) — creatinine is not listed. (Book p1003)

questions.sec: Variceal bleeds: determinants and natural history · p1004
questions.q: The main factor in variceal bleeds, as stated on p1004, is:
questions.exp: Determinants: main factor — variceal wall tension. (Book p1004)

questions.sec: Variceal bleeds: determinants and natural history · p1004
questions.q: Match the p1004 determinants of variceal bleeding — 1) Main factor  2) Vessel component  3) Pressure component  4) The bracketed note on diameter + pressure … A) Pressure  B) Variceal wall tension  C) Vessel diameter  D) Directly related to HVPG
questions.exp: Main factor: variceal wall tension; determined by vessel diameter + pressure; bracket: directly related to HVPG. (Book p1004)

questions.sec: Variceal bleeds: determinants and natural history · p1004
questions.q: The p1004 line ‘Gastric esophageal varices : 50% cause cirrhosis’ attributes varices to cirrhosis in what proportion (as printed)?
questions.exp: Causes: gastric esophageal varices : 50% cause cirrhosis (as printed). (Book p1004)

questions.sec: Variceal bleeds: determinants and natural history · p1004
questions.q: The development rate of varices in patients without varices, per p1004, is:
questions.exp: Causes: without varices development rate : 8% per year. (Book p1004)

questions.sec: Variceal bleeds: determinants and natural history · p1004
questions.q: The variceal hemorrhage occurrence rate given on p1004 is:
questions.exp: Causes: variceal hemorrhage occurrence rate : 5–15% per year. (Book p1004)

questions.sec: Variceal bleeds: determinants and natural history · p1004
questions.q: Match the p1004 risk-of-bleeding figures with the varix size — 1) Small varices (≤ 5 mm)  2) Large varices … A) 30%/year  B) < 10%/year
questions.exp: Risk of bleeding: small varices (≤ 5 mm) : < 10%/year; large varices : 30%/year. (Book p1004)

questions.sec: Variceal bleeds: determinants and natural history · p1004
questions.q: Mortality from variceal bleeding, as printed on p1004, is:
questions.exp: Causes: mortality from variceal bleeding : 15–30%. (Book p1004)

questions.sec: Variceal bleeds: determinants and natural history · p1004
questions.q: A cirrhotic is found to have large oesophageal varices on screening. Using only the p1004 figures, the pair that describes his annual bleed risk and the case-fatality if a bleed occurs is:

questions.sec: Acute variceal bleeding: the step-ladder · p1004
questions.q: A patient presents with acute variceal bleeding. The immediate access step in the p1004 flow is:

questions.sec: Acute variceal bleeding: the step-ladder · p1004
questions.q: The 1st-line vasoactive drug labelled (1st) in the p1004 flow is:
questions.exp: Terlipressin (1st) is the printed first-line arm; octreotide follows after the ‘>’ as the alternative. (Book p1004)

questions.sec: Acute variceal bleeding: the step-ladder · p1004
questions.q: The terlipressin regimen in the p1004 flow is:
opts: 2 mg Q6h × 7 days without a stat dose
2 mg stat dose → 2 mg Q6h × 48 hours

questions.sec: Acute variceal bleeding: the step-ladder · p1004
questions.q: The octreotide alternative in the p1004 flow is:

units.title: Clinical significance and pathogenesis of portal HTN
units.guide: Portal HTN can manifest with or without cirrhosis and leads to hepatic encephalopathy, variceal bleeding and ascites (1st sign of decompensation) → hepatorenal syndrome; jaundice + liver failure = decompensation with average survival without transplant printed as ‘a years’ (≈1 year) versus mean survival of 12 years without decompensation/transplant. Pathogenesis: portal venous pressure ≥ 12 mm Hg, sinusoidal pressure ≥ 6 mm Hg (clinically significant ≥ 10 mm Hg); cirrhosis (loss of fenestration, compression by nodules, ↑ septae) raises splenic pressure → splenomegaly (earliest clinical) and thrombocytopenia (earliest biochemical). The cirrhotic sinusoid diagram: collagen deposition in space of Disse, activation of hepatic stellate cells, constriction and defenestration of sinusoids; nodules and fibrous septae compress sinusoids → ↑ portal → ↑ splenic vein pressure (caput medusae = back flow of blood from portal veins).

units.title: Hepatic vasculature: the portal vein
units.guide: Portal vein: development — inferior segment of left and right vitelline veins joins to form it; formation — splenic vein + superior mesenteric vein join behind the neck of pancreas, 7.5 cm long, hilum posterior to hepatic (artery) and bile duct. High compliance, low resistance. Branching diagram: umbilical vein drains into left portal vein, cystic vein into right portal vein, 1st order = main trunk, 3rd order (Bifurcation), ‘…rd order (Entry)’ label garbled in print. Hepatic buffer response: hepatic ischaemia is rare d/t dual blood supply (portal vein, hepatic artery).

units.title: Sinusoidal vasoconstriction and the HVPG ladder
units.guide: Resistance due to (P = F × R; R↑ = P↑): mechanical — nodule compressing sinusoid; functional — ↓ intrasinusoidal NO → contraction of sinusoid → defenestration. HVPG table: 1–5 mm Hg normal; ≥ 10 mm Hg clinically significant portal hypertension; ≥ 12 mm Hg threshold for variceal rupture; ≥ 20 mm Hg ↑ risk of death.

units.title: Causes of portal HTN: pre-hepatic, post-hepatic, intrahepatic
units.guide: Pre-hepatic: 1st order portal vein occlusion AKA EHPVO — seen in 3–8 yr olds; severe upper GI bleed, massive splenomegaly, no cirrhosis (good prognosis); causes umbilical sepsis, splenic vein thrombosis (rare). Post-hepatic: (a) hepatic vein obstruction AKA Budd–Chiari (classical: ascites + hepatomegaly); (b) right heart failure — tricuspid regurgitation, restrictive cardiomyopathy, constrictive pericarditis (↑ JVP). Intrahepatic (3rd order portal vein): pre-sinusoidal — NCPF/idiopathic portal hypertension (young adult, upper GI bleed, splenomegaly, cirrhosis rare), schistosomiasis, sarcoidosis; post-sinusoidal — sinusoidal obstruction syndrome/veno-occlusive disease a/w post-hematopoietic stem cell transplant following myeloablative alkylating therapy, symptoms 10–30 days after; sinusoidal — cirrhosis.

units.title: Work-up of portal HTN and the WHVP/FHVP/HVPG table
units.guide: Flow: patient with risk factors for chronic hepatitis → deranged LFT + USG (fatty liver + negative serology, AST/ALT < 150) → confirms chronic hepatitis (NASH) → Fibroscan 13.5 kPa → cirrhosis → splenomegaly (+), ↓ platelet → portal HTN (+) → quantity with HVPG / endoscopy. HVPG = WHVP − FHVP (expansion line prints ‘FWVP: free hepatic venous pressure’). Table: prehepatic & presinusoidal — all normal; sinusoidal & postsinusoidal — WHVP ↑, FHVP normal, HVPG ↑; unlabeled row — WHVP ↑, FHVP ↑ (hepatic vein cannot be cannulated), HVPG normal. HVPG > 10 mm Hg → Rx non-selective β-blocker carvedilol (best).

units.title: Endoscopy, EVL indications and modified Child–Pugh
units.guide: Endoscopy: large varices → non-selective β-blocker carvedilol (best); mild/moderate varices → conservative management. Indications for endoscopic variceal ligation: intolerant to β-blocker therapy (asthma, COPD); β-blockers contraindicated (severe bradycardia); target HVPG not achieved with β-blocker. Modified Child–Pugh: parameters — ascites, encephalopathy, bilirubin, albumin, prothrombin time (seconds increased); classes A, B, C with B + C bracketed as ‘requires transplant’.

units.title: Variceal bleeds: determinants and natural history
units.guide: Main factor: variceal wall tension, determined by vessel diameter + pressure, directly related to HVPG. Causes/epidemiology: gastric esophageal varices 50% cause cirrhosis (as printed); without-varices development rate 8%/year; variceal hemorrhage occurrence 5–15%/year; risk of bleeding — small varices (≤ 5 mm) < 10%/year, large varices 30%/year; mortality from variceal bleeding 15–30%.

units.title: Acute variceal bleeding: the step-ladder
units.guide: Bleeding → a large bore IV cannulas; terlipressin (1st) stat dose → 2 mg Q6h × 48 hours (print shows ‘a mg’); alternative (>) IV octreotide 50 µg stat → 50 µg/hour; box — start antibiotics, replace blood volume, intubation to be considered; upon failure → endoscopy: variceal ligation or sclerotherapy; upon failure → TIPSS (transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt).
